0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
There is a letter that reads like a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front, and a father’s farewell to his son — all at once. Paul writes 2 Timothy from a Roman dungeon, by tradition the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. He has already stood before Nero’s tribunal; he expects to stand there again, and this time he does not expect to survive. He has been abandoned by most of his colleagues. Demas has gone back to the world. The churches of Asia have turned away. The winter is coming and he has no cloak. Only Luke is with him.

And yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith. Paul is not finished. He is fighting, praying, thinking, teaching to the last. He writes to Timothy — the son of his heart, the young man he circumcised and took on mission, who is now in Ephesus struggling with false teachers and the creeping temptation to soft-pedal the gospel for the sake of peace — and he writes with the urgency of a man who knows the window is closing. Guard the deposit. Don’t be ashamed. Endure suffering. Preach the word. These are not polite suggestions; they are dying instructions.

The letter is the most personal in the Pauline corpus. More than anywhere else we see Paul the man: Paul who remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him, who is comforted by Onesiphorus’s courage, who feels the sting of Alexander’s opposition, who in his final lines sends greetings from people whose names he has not forgotten. The great apostle is a human being who is cold, lonely, and facing death — and whose faith in the Jesus who appears in this letter (“remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead”) is, in the end, the only thing that has not shaken.

Is this really Paul’s last letter? Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome after two years under guard (Acts 28:30). The early church believed he was released, travelled again, and was arrested a second time under Nero, and this letter fits that setting: he has had a first defense (4:16), he expects to die (4:6), and he writes from harsher chains than in Acts. It was probably written around AD 64–67, shortly before his execution.

The letter is addressed to the minister, but it speaks to every Christian who must hold something precious in a world that does not want it. The deposit Paul entrusts to Timothy — the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen — is the same deposit entrusted to every generation of the church. Guard it. Pass it on. It is worth dying for. Paul’s life proves the claim.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
These are Paul’s last written words. He is in prison in Rome and expects to die (4:6). He writes to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith, who is gifted, sincere and timid. Paul remembers his tears and his believing mother and grandmother, and then presses the charge: rekindle God’s gift, for God gave not a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-control. Do not be ashamed of the gospel or of me; share in suffering by God’s power.

The ground of courage is the gospel itself (vv. 9–10): God saved us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began, and Christ has abolished death. So Paul can say, “I know whom I have believed.” The chapter ends with a choice of examples: all Asia, which turned away, and Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found Paul and was not ashamed of his chains.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, an apostle by God’s will for the sake of the promise of life in Christ, writes to Timothy, his dear son, with grace, mercy and peace. This is his last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation because none is in view: this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time, and ‘mercy’ appears in the greeting as it does only in the letters to Timothy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul calls himself the Lord's prisoner, not Rome's (v.8; cf. Eph 3:1).

Now: A man facing execution opens his last letter with ‘the promise of the life’ — the letter's whole argument in its first sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, facing death, writes as an apostle of the promise of life in Christ to his beloved son Timothy.

Where it comes from. A Roman prison, with execution expected. These are the last words we have from Paul.

The promise of life. A man on death row names his commission in terms of life. That is the letter’s argument in its first sentence.

By God’s will. Whatever a court decides, his appointment came from somewhere no court can reach.

Beloved child. In the first letter, “true child”, set against counterfeits. Here the edge has gone. He is writing to someone he loves.

Mercy. Paul puts it in a greeting only in the letters to Timothy. Timothy will need it.

For worship. The promise of life in Christ is not cancelled by a death sentence. It is what makes one bearable.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome as he expected to die, probably in the mid 60s AD under Nero. Timothy was probably still in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God, whom he serves with a clear conscience, and prays for Timothy constantly, remembering his tears at parting and longing to see him. He recalls Timothy’s sincere faith, first seen in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. So he urges him to rekindle God’s gift given through the laying on of Paul’s hands, for God gave a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control. Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul the prisoner, but share in suffering, relying on God, who saved and called us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began and now revealed in Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. For this gospel Paul suffers unashamed, sure that God will guard what he has entrusted. Timothy is to hold to the pattern of sound teaching and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paul has entrusted his deposit to God, who is able to guard it (v.12); God has entrusted a deposit to Timothy, who must guard it by the indwelling Spirit (v.14). And behind both stands the grace given in Christ before the ages began, by the Saviour who abolished death (vv.9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The faith came to Timothy through his grandmother and mother (v.5; Acts 16:1), long before any laying on of hands.

Now: To a timid man Paul names what he has been given — power, love and a sound mind (v.7) — rather than telling him to feel braver.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God and longs to see Timothy, remembering his tears.

My ancestors. Paul does not treat his Jewish heritage as a false start. The God he serves is the God of his fathers; the gospel is what that God promised.

A clear conscience. The test he set in 1 Timothy 1:5, 19, now quietly claimed: a man at the end with nothing outstanding.

Night and day. In a cell with empty hours, an old man prays for his friend at three in the morning.

Your tears. A parting, probably when Paul was taken. He treasures the memory and does not call the tears weakness.

That I may be filled with joy. Paul, facing death calmly, admits he needs Timothy. Contentment never meant needing nobody.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone you miss them. It is not weakness; Paul did.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy’s sincere faith first lived in his grandmother and mother.

Sincere. Anypokritos, un-masked. Whatever his timidity, Timothy’s faith is real.

Three generations. His father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), probably not a believer. The faith came down the female line.

How faith travels. Two letters on elders and ordination, and the man Paul trusts with everything was formed by two women teaching a child at home (3:15). Nobody laid hands on Lois. She taught her daughter, who taught her son.

Dwells. Takes up residence. Faith is not visiting; it lives there.

I am sure. Some people need someone else to tell them their faith is real.

On a Tuesday. Grandparents, single mothers, mothers with unbelieving husbands: your bedtime Bible stories may be the most important ministry in the church.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s father was a Greek; his faith came through his mother’s side.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must fan into flame God’s gift, for God gave us a spirit of power, love and self-control, not fear.

Fan into flame. Embers, not ashes. The gift has not gone out; it needs air. A gentle diagnosis of a man burnt low under long pressure.

My hands. In 1 Timothy 4:14, the elders’ hands. Both are true; here Paul presses the personal tie as he faces death.

Not of fear. Deilia: cowardice, shrinking from duty. Paul names it, so it was there. Scripture records a leader’s timidity without embarrassment.

Three gifts. Power, because the task is beyond him. Love, because fear makes us self-protective and love gets us outside ourselves. Self-control, a sound mind, because fear distorts judgement.

What it does not mean. Not that every feeling of fear is sin. Many faithful believers feel afraid, and some anxiety has bodily causes and needs treatment. Paul means the shrinking back from Christ’s call. The Spirit enables us to act faithfully while afraid.

Can a gift be lost? It can be neglected and dimmed. It is kept bright by use.

On a Tuesday. Paul does not tell the frightened to feel braver. He tells them what they have been given. Do the next faithful thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul, but share in suffering by God’s power.

Ashamed. The chapter’s word (vv. 8, 12, 16). Shame is the pressure Timothy faces.

Of the message. Announcing a crucified provincial as Lord. Crucifixion was for slaves and rebels (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Of me. The real difficulty. Paul awaits execution; everyone in Asia has backed away (v. 15).

His prisoner. The custody is Rome’s; the ownership is the Lord’s.

Suffer together. Not “be brave on your own”, but “come and share this”.

By the power of God. Not by Timothy’s resolve. The spirit of power (v. 7) is spent here.

On a Tuesday. Being linked publicly with an unpopular Christian, or with Christ, will cost you. Do it anyway, leaning on God’s strength.

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved and called us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began and now revealed.

Not our works. Saved and called by God, for his own reasons.

Before the ages. Grace was not only planned but given to us in Christ before time. Nothing done since can be the reason.

Election. Arminian Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But grace given before the ages and not because of anything in us points to God’s free choice, with faith itself his gift. The more likely reading is that election rests on his purpose alone.

Appearing. Epiphaneia: a king’s public arrival. The hidden purpose came out in Christ.

Abolished death. Made it inoperative, disarmed it. Written in the past tense by a man awaiting execution. Death still happens; it no longer works.

Brought to light. Immortality, which philosophers argued over, is now lit up by an event: the resurrection.

For worship. The argument to the frightened is not “be brave” but “death has been abolished; what exactly can they threaten you with?”

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul suffers for this gospel unashamed, for he knows whom he has believed and that God will guard what is entrusted.

Why I suffer. Suffering is not an interruption of the call; it follows from it.

I am not ashamed. He does not ask Timothy to bear what he is privately embarrassed by.

Whom, not what. At the end Paul leans not on the soundness of his doctrine, though he fought for it, but on the person it is about.

What has been entrusted. Either what Paul entrusted to God (his life, his work) or what God entrusted to Paul (the gospel, as in v. 14). Most take the first here: everything a man cannot hold himself, lodged with someone who can.

Kept to the end? Arminian Christians hold that a believer may fail to persevere. Believers must persevere, but it is God who keeps them (John 10:28; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). That is why Paul faces death unashamed.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “of the Gentiles” after “teacher” in v. 11, probably from 1 Timothy 2:7. The shorter text is earlier.

On a Tuesday. When doctrine feels thin in a crisis, pray to the person, not the proposition: “I know whom I have believed.”

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must hold to the pattern of sound words and guard the deposit by the Spirit.

Pattern. Hypotypōsis, an outline to work from. Not Paul’s sentences verbatim, but the shape.

Heard from me. The chain the letter traces: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others (2:2).

In faith and love. Doctrine held without them becomes what the Ephesian teachers had: correct-sounding and quarrelsome.

The deposit. Parathēkē, property left in trust, to be returned as received, not improved.

By the Spirit. A timid man, a dying mentor, a deserting province. The guarding is done by someone who lives inside the guard.

Two deposits. Paul entrusts to God (v. 12); God entrusts to Timothy (v. 14). The strength in both comes from God.

On a Tuesday. When you teach your children or your class, hand on the faith as you received it, without “improving” it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul contrasts two kinds of friend. Everyone in the province of Asia has turned away from him, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. But Onesiphorus often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains; in Rome he searched hard until he found Paul, as he had served him in Ephesus. Paul prays that the Lord will show mercy to his household and to him on that day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

‘Ashamed’ runs through the chapter (vv.8, 12, 16). The turning away of verse 15 was most likely personal desertion of a dangerous prisoner rather than apostasy — a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia, the scene of Paul's most fruitful work (Acts 19:10), turned away at the end.

Now: Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found a condemned man (v.17) — an answer to shame available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All in Asia have turned away from Paul.

Asia. The province of Ephesus, where Paul taught for three years until all the region heard the word (Acts 19:10). His most fruitful work, and at the end they turned away.

All. A generalisation (the next verse names an exception), but it is how it felt from the cell.

Desertion, not apostasy. Most likely personal: association with a man on a capital charge was dangerous. A more ordinary failure, and so a more likely one for us.

Two names. Known only for this. A sobering way to be remembered.

Honest cost. Paul is about to ask Timothy to come. He tells him first that everyone else has declined.

On a Tuesday. When a Christian friend is in disgrace, illness or prison, will you be one of the “all” or the exception?
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul’s chains, but searched for him and refreshed him.

Refreshed. To cool, like shade or water. Often, not once.

Not ashamed of my chains. The chapter’s word, answered. Others could not stomach the visible, incriminating fact of the chains.

Searched. Rome had perhaps a million people. Asking after a man on a capital charge drew official attention. He kept asking until he found him.

Find mercy. He sought Paul out; may he be found by mercy.

Prayer for the dead? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse, with 2 Maccabees 12, to support prayer for the dead and purgatory. But it is not clear that Onesiphorus had died; he may simply have been away. Even if he had, Paul voices a wish about the judgment, not a prayer to change his state. Scripture never commands prayer for the dead, and says death is followed by judgment (Hebrews 9:27).

On a Tuesday. Onesiphorus held no office we know of. He turned up, repeatedly, and was not embarrassed to be seen there. Anyone can do that.

But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.<sup>13</sup>Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.<sup>15</sup>You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.<sup>16</sup>May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains,<sup>17</sup>but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me—<sup>18</sup>may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.

2.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer: The Shape of Gospel Ministry
2.overview:
Paul tells Timothy what gospel ministry is like. Be strengthened by grace, and hand the teaching on to reliable people who will teach others. Endure like a soldier, train like an athlete, labour like a farmer. Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead: Paul is chained, but God’s word is not. A trustworthy saying holds it together: if we died with him we will live with him; if we are faithless, he remains faithful.

The second half turns to false teaching. Avoid word-fights, which ruin the listeners. Cut the word of truth straight. Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened, but God’s foundation stands: “The Lord knows those who are his.” Cleanse yourself to be useful to the Master, run from youthful passions with others who seek God, and correct opponents gently, because repentance is God’s gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges Timothy to draw strength from the grace that is in Christ and to hand on the teaching he received to reliable people who will teach others in turn. He must be ready to suffer, like a soldier who stays free of civilian distractions to please his commander, an athlete who keeps the rules to win, and a farmer who works hard and so gets the first of the harvest. He is to keep Jesus Christ in mind, risen from the dead and descended from David, the gospel for which Paul is in chains like a criminal, though God’s message cannot be chained. Paul endures it all for the sake of God’s chosen people, that they too may be saved. A reliable saying sums it up: those who die with Christ will live with him, those who endure will reign with him, those who disown him will be disowned, but even when we are unfaithful he stays faithful, because he cannot be untrue to himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Broken Symmetry of Verse 13

The hymn's first three lines match our action with his response; the fourth breaks the pattern in our favour — we are faithless, he remains faithful — grounded not in our sincerity but in his nature: ‘he cannot deny himself’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: From a death cell Paul arranges for the deposit to pass through four generations of faithful men (v.2).

Now: Soldier, athlete, farmer (vv.3–6): singleness, discipline and patience — and the word of God is not bound (v.9).

verseByVerse.quote: You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strengthened by grace, Timothy must entrust the apostolic teaching to faithful people who will teach others.

Be strengthened. Passive. Paul does not tell a timid man to be strong, but to let grace make him strong. Grace pardons, and grace powers.

Four links. Christ to Paul, Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, faithful men to others. From a death cell, Paul arranges for the gospel to outlive him by three hands.

Faithful. Not gifted, clever or impressive: reliable. And able to pass it on; a man who only receives is a dead end.

Apostolic succession? Some churches teach that authority passes through an unbroken line of bishops. But what is passed on here is teaching. The succession that matters is faithfulness to the apostles’ doctrine, now written in Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Who are you passing the faith to? Pick one younger believer and read the Bible with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a soldier, he must share in suffering and avoid entanglements.

Entangled. Woven into. Not sinful things but ordinary ones: business, property. A soldier accepts limits on how much of ordinary life he carries, because he can be moved at any hour.

One person to please. A relief for Timothy, surrounded by people with opinions. One commanding officer.

What it does not mean. Not permission to neglect family or work; Paul insists a man provide for his household (1 Timothy 5:8). It warns against being so wrapped in comfort and possessions that you cannot move when the order comes.

On a Tuesday. Could you say yes tomorrow if God called you to something costly? What would hold you back?

verseByVerse.quote: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like an athlete and a farmer, he must compete by the rules and work hard.

By the rules. In the Greek games this included the required training beforehand. Effort alone does not qualify; there is a right way to do the work, and results got the wrong way earn nothing.

The farmer. He adds time. Battles are decided in a day, races in an afternoon. A farmer works for months seeing nothing, and if he stops because nothing shows, there is no harvest.

Three pictures. Soldier: single aim. Athlete: discipline. Farmer: patience. Timothy needed the third most.

Think, and be given. Hard thinking is commanded; understanding is God’s gift. Neither cancels the other.

On a Tuesday. Sunday-school teachers, parents, pastors in small churches: you are farmers. Keep sowing.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember Jesus Christ, risen and descended from David; the word of God is not chained.

Two clauses. Risen, so he is Lord and death is beaten. David’s offspring, so he is truly human and God’s promises are kept.

Remember. Under pressure we forget what we know perfectly well. The cure is recollection, which is what the Lord’s Supper is for.

A criminal. Kakourgos, the word for the men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:32).

Not bound. Rome can hold the apostle and do nothing to the message. The sentence written in that cell has travelled further than anyone who put him there.

For worship. Preachers can be silenced, churches closed, Bibles confiscated. No one has ever imprisoned the word.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul endures everything for the elect, that they may obtain salvation.

Everything. Not rhetoric from this man: floggings, stonings, shipwreck, and now a death cell.

For the elect. For people, most of whom he has never met. His suffering is not only borne but spent on someone.

Why bother, if God has chosen? Because election is not a reason for inaction but the reason action is worthwhile. Paul knows God has a people, so his labour is not a gamble; he does not know who they are, so he preaches to all (Acts 18:9–10). God ordains the means as well as the end.

Eternal glory. Everything endured, weighed against what it gains.

On a Tuesday. Evangelism is not a lottery. Speak to your neighbour in the confidence that God has people still to call.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trustworthy saying: dying with him we will live; enduring we will reign; denying him he will deny us; yet he remains faithful.

A hymn. Four balanced lines.

Died with him. Past: union with Christ at conversion. The living is sure.

Endure, reign. Present endurance, and a promise not of survival but of reigning.

Deny. Jesus’ own word (Matthew 10:33). Settled, final denial has a settled answer.

The broken pattern. The first three lines match our act with his response. The fourth does not: we are faithless, and he is faithful. The symmetry fails in our favour.

Can a true Christian deny Christ and be lost? Arminian Christians read line three as a warning that real believers may fall away. But Peter denied Christ and was restored, so it cannot mean every failure. It describes final, settled repudiation, which shows such a person never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). To be faithless is to fail; to deny is to disown.

He cannot deny himself. His faithfulness rests on his nature, not our sincerity.

For worship. If you keep collapsing, this line is for you.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth of the “trustworthy sayings,” perhaps an early hymn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy must keep warning the church, before God, against quarrelling over words, which ruins those who listen. He should work to be a worker God approves, unashamed, teaching the message of truth accurately, and avoid empty, irreverent talk, which spreads like an infection; Hymenaeus and Philetus, for instance, are upsetting people’s faith by claiming the resurrection has already happened. Still, God’s foundation stands firm, sealed with two truths: the Lord knows his own, and those who call on his name must turn from evil. Like household utensils, people can be fit for honourable use if they cleanse themselves. Timothy should run from youthful desires and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace with sincere believers, and refuse foolish arguments. The Lord’s servant must not fight but be kind, able to teach and patient, gently correcting opponents in the hope that God will grant them repentance and they will escape the devil’s snare.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cutting Straight

‘Rightly handling’ (v.15) is to cut straight, like a craftsman whose cut cannot be undone: accuracy, not eloquence. And God's foundation bears two seals (v.19) — the Lord knows his own, and those who name him depart from iniquity.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hymenaeus, already disciplined (1 Tim 1:20), was still teaching that the resurrection had come — wrecking the hope of the grieving first.

Now: Word-fights damage the hearers (v.14); cleanse yourself rather than audit the house (v.21); and correct with gentleness, since repentance is God's to grant (v.25).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must warn people against quarrelling about words.

Word-fights. Logomachein, the same disease as at Ephesus (1 Timothy 6:4).

Before God. Oath language. Paul does not treat it as a minor irritation.

Ruins the hearers. Katastrophē. Not the fighters, who are often enjoying themselves, but the people in the room who did not want the fight. The new believer learns that Christianity is a thing people shout about.

What it does not mean. Not that words do not matter; v. 15 demands accuracy. It forbids quarrelling over them for its own sake.

On a Tuesday. Before posting that theological reply online, ask: who will be reading, and what will they learn?

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must aim to be an approved worker, rightly handling the word of truth.

To God. Not the congregation or the critics. One audience.

Approved. Dokimos, metal tested and passed.

No need to be ashamed. The chapter-one word reversed: a craftsman looking at his work without apology.

Cut straight. Orthotomeō. Paul was a tentmaker: the material is costly, the cut irreversible, and a wandering line ruins the piece. The aim is accuracy, not eloquence: giving what the text says, not what the preacher wishes.

Rightly dividing? The KJV’s “rightly dividing” has been taken by some to mean dividing Scripture into dispensations. The verb means handling correctly, cutting a straight line. Paul calls for accurate teaching, not a scheme of divisions.

On a Tuesday. When you quote a verse to someone, check the context first. Cut straight.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Irreverent babble spreads like gangrene, as with those who say the resurrection is past.

Avoid. Not refute: some error is not worth the dignity of debate.

More and more. Error does not settle; each step makes the next thinkable.

Gangrene. It spreads by contact, cannot be reasoned with, and is treated by cutting away.

Hymenaeus. Disciplined in 1 Timothy 1:20 and still at it, now with a colleague. Scripture admits discipline does not always work.

Already happened. Probably spiritualised: resurrection means new life now, and nothing bodily is coming. It sounds advanced and requires no waiting.

Today’s version. Full preterism holds that Christ’s return and the resurrection were fulfilled in AD 70. Paul’s verdict applies: it swerves from the truth. The resurrection of the body is still to come.

Upsetting faith. If it has already happened, the dead have missed it and the suffering have nothing coming. It lands on the grieving first.

verseByVerse.quote: But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s firm foundation stands: the Lord knows those who are his, and they must turn from evil.

A foundation stone. Inscribed, as ancient stones were, with two lines facing opposite ways.

God’s side. From Numbers 16:5, Moses’ answer when Korah’s rebellion made it unclear who belonged to God. Exactly Timothy’s situation. The register is not kept by us. You may have been badly wrong about someone; God is not.

Our side. The name commits you to leave the sin.

Both lines. Assurance rests on God’s knowledge, not our performance; and the evidence that we belong is our turning from sin. A foundation with one line will not hold the building.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “the name of Christ”. “Of the Lord” is earlier and better attested; the meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. After a church scandal, rest on the first line and act on the second.
verseByVerse.note: The first saying echoes the rebellion of Korah; the second gathers the sense of Moses’ warning to leave the rebels’ tents.

parallels.desc: the LORD will show who is his
Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever cleanses himself will be a vessel for honourable use.

A great house. Fine ware for the table, common ware for the yard. The church, God’s household, contains both. False teachers inside do not prove it false.

Cleanse yourself. Reflexive. Paul does not tell Timothy to audit the house and sort everyone. Attend to yourself.

Not fixed. A vessel can change category. No one is stuck being clay.

Useful. Not admired or prominent: picked up and used by the owner.

On a Tuesday. Is there one habit you need to cleanse from, so God can use you without spilling what he puts in you?

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace with fellow believers.

Flee and pursue. As at 1 Timothy 6:11. Avoidance alone leaves a vacuum.

Youthful passions. Sexual temptation certainly (1 Timothy 5:2). But the next verse is about quarrels, so it includes the young man’s appetite for argument, the need to be right, and impatience to make a mark.

Peace. The pointed one in a chapter about word-fights.

With others. Not a solo pursuit. Paul’s answer to corrosive company is not isolation but better company inside the church.

On a Tuesday. You cannot always choose your church; you can choose who you spend your time with in it. Choose people who pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s servant must be kind, patient and gentle with opponents, for God may grant them repentance.

Breed. A birth word. Such arguments keep producing quarrels.

The portrait. Not quarrelsome, kind to all, including opponents, able to teach, bearing wrongs without retaliating.

Correct gently. Both halves: he does correct, and he does it gently. Most of us manage one.

God may grant repentance. Repentance is God’s gift, not the prize of winning an argument. So gentleness is not weakness: you cannot argue anyone into repentance.

Captured. Paul sees his opponents not as villains but as trapped, doing another’s will while thinking it their own. Hence gentleness.

On a Tuesday. When someone you love has embraced error, pray for God to grant repentance, and speak the truth kindly.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>2</sup>and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.<sup>3</sup>Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.<sup>4</sup>No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.<sup>5</sup>An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.<sup>6</sup>It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops.<sup>7</sup>Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.<sup>8</sup>Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel,<sup>9</sup>for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!<sup>10</sup>Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.<sup>11</sup>The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him;<sup>12</sup>if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us;<sup>13</sup>if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.<sup>14</sup>Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.<sup>15</sup>Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.<sup>16</sup>But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness,<sup>17</sup>and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus,<sup>18</sup>who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.<sup>19</sup>But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."<sup>20</sup>Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable.<sup>21</sup>Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.<sup>22</sup>So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.<sup>23</sup>Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels.<sup>24</sup>And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil,<sup>25</sup>correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth,<sup>26</sup>and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.

3.title: Perilous Times and the God-Breathed Word
3.overview:
Paul warns that the last days, which began with Christ, will bring savage times. His list of vices is framed by love of self and love of pleasure, and it describes not pagans but religious people: “having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power”. Such people worm into homes and prey on the vulnerable, always teaching and never bringing anyone to the truth. Like Pharaoh’s magicians, they imitate, and like them they will be exposed.

Against this, Timothy has three anchors: Paul’s example of teaching, life and suffering; the people who taught him from childhood; and the Scriptures themselves. All Scripture is breathed out by God and makes the man of God complete. The answer to savage times is not innovation but a book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Godlessness in the Last Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns that the last days will be hard times. People will love themselves and money, be proud, abusive, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, treacherous, reckless and conceited, loving pleasure rather than God, keeping an outward form of godliness while denying its power. Timothy must avoid such people. Some worm their way into homes and gain influence over weak women burdened with sins, always learning but never reaching the truth. Like Jannes and Jambres, Pharaoh’s magicians who opposed Moses, they oppose the truth, but their folly will be exposed.
verseByVerse.theology:
What ‘the Last Days’ Means

The last days began with Christ (Acts 2:16-17; Heb 1:2), and Timothy was living in them. The list's final item puts the whole catalogue inside the church: the outline of godliness kept while its power is denied (v.5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The vices are framed by self-love and pleasure-love (vv.2, 4) and are mostly relational collapse rather than false doctrine.

Now: Imitation has a ceiling: Pharaoh's magicians could not keep pace for long (v.9; Exod 8:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last days, the age between Christ’s comings, will bring difficult times.

The last days. Not a remote future. They began with Christ (Acts 2:16–17; Hebrews 1:2). Timothy is told to avoid such people (v. 5), so they were already about.

Difficulty. Chalepos, used elsewhere only of the demoniacs “so fierce” no one could pass (Matthew 8:28). Times with teeth in them.

Seasons. Kairoi: even the hard stretches belong to a calendar God keeps.

Understand this. Paul tells people in advance (1 Thessalonians 3:4). A Christian told to expect hard times is not destroyed by them; one promised an easy road may be.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shocked by the news, or by the church. You were warned.
verseByVerse.note: The “last days” began with Christ’s first coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
People will be lovers of self, money and pleasure rather than lovers of God.

The frame. It opens with lovers of self and closes with lovers of pleasure. Five words are built on philos, “lover”. It is a list about disordered love.

Relational collapse. Disobedient to parents, ungrateful, astorgoi (without the natural affection that binds families), aspondoi (a treaty word: refusing any truce, unwilling to accept an apology).

Not dramatic. Almost nothing about false doctrine or outside persecution. Ordinary relationships coming apart. Recognisable.

Self-love and self-esteem. Paul condemns putting self at the centre, not ordinary self-care, which Jesus assumes (Matthew 22:39). The modern push for self-esteem can feed the very self-love Paul describes. The gospel gives something better: a secure identity in Christ that frees us to forget ourselves.

On a Tuesday. Which word on the list describes your last week? Start there.

verseByVerse.quote: having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will keep the outward form of godliness but deny its power; avoid them.

Inside the church. Verses 2–4 could describe pagan Ephesus. This clause puts the whole list in the pews.

Appearance. Morphōsis: the outline. They attend, use the vocabulary, and would be offended to be called unbelievers.

Denying its power. Not denying the creed, which they may recite well, but denying in practice that godliness changes anything.

Avoid. Not reform them or argue them down.

What it does not mean. Not struggling Christians whose lives are a mess; we bear with them. Paul means settled hypocrisy. Such people are not to become a young minister’s endless project.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether your faith has power in your home, not only form in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such teachers prey on vulnerable people who are always learning but never arriving at the truth.

Creep in. Entry by stealth. Capture. A war word: to take prisoner (compare 2:26).

Households. Where the churches met and where women spent their days.

Weak women. A diminutive, not kind. But this is not contempt for women; Paul has just named Lois and Eunice (1:5). He describes particular people being exploited: carrying guilt, pulled in several directions. That is the profile predators look for.

Always learning. Not a failure of effort. Endless teaching that never arrives is what such teachers want, because someone who arrives no longer needs them.

On a Tuesday. Beware any teacher, online or in person, who keeps you dependent rather than pointing you to Christ and Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Moses’ opponents, they resist the truth, and their folly will be exposed.

Jannes and Jambres. Not named in Exodus; Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh’s magicians (Exodus 7:11–12). Paul uses a tradition his readers knew.

Imitation. The magicians did not deny Moses; they copied him. So with those who have the outline of godliness.

Disqualified. Adokimos, the failed assay, against Timothy “approved” (2:15).

Not very far. Not a promise of brevity, but of a ceiling. The magicians kept pace for two plagues, then could not produce gnats: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19).

On a Tuesday. When error seems to be winning, wait. Imitation runs out, usually sooner than we fear.
verseByVerse.note: Jannes and Jambres are not named in Exodus; Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh’s magicians.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Scripture and the Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds Timothy that he has closely followed Paul’s teaching, way of life, aims, faith, patience, love and perseverance, and his sufferings in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, from all of which the Lord delivered him. Anyone determined to live a godly life in Christ will meet persecution, while deceivers grow worse. Timothy must stay with what he has learned and been convinced of, remembering his teachers and the Scriptures he has known since childhood, which can make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ. Every part of Scripture comes from the breath of God and is useful for teaching, for exposing error, for setting things right and for training in righteous living, so that God’s servant is thoroughly prepared for every good task.
verseByVerse.theology:
Breathed Out by God

Scripture is God-breathed (v.16) — proceeding from him, not dictated, with its writers genuinely speaking as they were carried along (2 Pet 1:21) — and it teaches, reproves, corrects and trains, so that the man of God is complete.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (v.11) were the towns of the first journey, and Lystra was Timothy's home (Acts 14:19; 16:1).

Now: Opposition for godliness (v.12) is not evidence of failure; its absence is the thing worth examining.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy has followed Paul’s teaching, life and sufferings, and the Lord rescued Paul from them all.

You, however. Against the imitators, one young man who has seen the real thing.

One and eight. One item of teaching, eight of life. Timothy learned Paul on the road more than in the lecture hall.

Lystra. Timothy’s home town (Acts 16:1), where Paul was stoned and left for dead, then got up and went back in (Acts 14:19–20). A boy may have watched.

Rescued. Written by a man who knows he will not be rescued this time. The rescues were real. That God does not always deliver does not mean he never does, and Paul will say the Lord will bring him safely into his kingdom (4:18). Death completes the rescue.

On a Tuesday. Someone younger is watching how you handle suffering. Let them see faith.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted, while deceivers go from bad to worse.

All. One of the least qualified sentences in the New Testament.

Desire. The wanting draws fire, not the achievement.

Read honestly. Most believers in comfortable countries will not be imprisoned, and pretending otherwise cheapens the word for those who are. But persecution has a range: a family that finds you embarrassing, a promotion lost, friendships cooling, being thought narrow.

Have I done wrong? Opposition for godliness is not evidence of failure. Its total absence may be worth examining.

Deceiving and deceived. The liar becomes unable to tell. The state cannot be detected from inside, which is frightening.

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians by name. Their suffering is what this verse looks like at full strength.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must continue in what he learned, and in the Scriptures he has known from childhood, which make wise for salvation.

Continue. Stay put. Against people always learning and never arriving, the instruction is not to innovate.

From whom. Weigh the teaching by the people it came through: Paul, Lois, Eunice. Their lives were evidence.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “from whom” in the singular (Paul alone). The plural is better attested and fits 1:5: Timothy had several teachers.

From childhood. From infancy. Two women taught a small boy the Old Testament, and decades later it is why he will hold.

Through faith in Christ. Scripture does not save by being read. It makes wise for salvation by pointing to Christ (John 5:39). Without the pointing, a man can know it well and not be saved, like many of Paul’s opponents.

On a Tuesday. Read the Bible with your children or grandchildren tonight. You may be preparing a Timothy.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Scripture is breathed out by God and useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness.

Breathed out. Theopneustos, perhaps Paul’s own coinage. Not “breathed into”, as if God enlivened human documents, but breathed out, as breath comes from a speaker. A claim about origin, not about the writers’ feelings.

Not dictation. Luke researched (Luke 1:3); Paul argues; David weeps. The writers truly spoke, carried along by the Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).

A translation question. Some render it “every inspired Scripture is also useful”, implying some may not be. The ESV’s reading is more natural Greek and fits Paul’s point: all of it.

All. Genealogies, building plans, lament psalms. And the New Testament too: Peter counts Paul’s letters with “the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16), and Paul quotes Luke 10:7 as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18).

Four uses. Teaching (what is true), reproof (where you are wrong), correction (putting you upright), training (long formation). It does not stop at diagnosis. A reader who only ever feels rebuked is using half the Bible.

Complete. Fully furnished. Against savage times, Paul hands his successor a book, sufficient for everything God asks.

Views. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches place church tradition alongside Scripture as a rule of faith. This verse makes Scripture sufficient to equip the man of God; tradition is valued but tested by it. And what God breathes out does not mislead: the doctrine of inerrancy.

For worship. When you open your Bible, God is speaking.

4.title: Preach the Word: The Commission, the Crown, and the Cloak
4.overview:
Paul’s last chapter has two halves. First the charge, sworn before the Judge of the living and the dead: preach the word, in season and out, because people will gather teachers who tell them what they want to hear. Keep your head, endure, evangelise, finish your ministry. Then Paul’s own finish: he is being poured out like a drink offering, he has fought the good fight and kept the faith, and a crown is waiting, for him and for all who love Christ’s appearing.

The second half is the most human passage Paul wrote. Demas has left, loving this world. Only Luke remains. Bring Mark, once a deserter, now useful. Bring my cloak and my books. At my hearing everyone abandoned me, but the Lord stood by me. The last word Paul wrote is “grace”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Preach the Word, and Finish the Race
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the judgement of Christ in view, Paul gives Timothy his final charge: proclaim the message, be ready whether the moment seems right or not, and correct, warn and encourage with great patience and careful teaching. People will soon refuse healthy doctrine and collect teachers who tell them what they want to hear, turning to myths. Timothy must stay steady, accept hardship, do the work of an evangelist and complete his ministry. Paul himself is near the end: his life is being poured out as an offering and his departure is at hand. He has fought well, finished the course and kept faith, and he looks forward to the crown of righteousness the Lord will give him on the last day, and to everyone who has longed for Christ’s appearing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Charge, and the Steward's Report

Paul swears Timothy before the court that will judge both him and Nero (v.1), and his ‘I have kept the faith’ (v.7) is a steward's report, not a boast. The crown is for all who have loved Christ's appearing (v.8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The itch is in the hearers' ears (v.3): they assemble teachers to suit themselves.

Now: When did one of your teachers last tell you something you did not want to hear?

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God and Christ, the coming judge, Timothy must preach the word in season and out of season.

A higher court. Paul awaits a Roman verdict. He swears Timothy before the court that will judge both Paul and Nero.

Preach. The herald’s verb: announce what you were given. A herald does not compose or improve the message.

The word. The deposit, not the preacher’s own thoughts about it.

In season and out. There will be plenty of “out”. Be standing by anyway.

Three verbs. Reprove and rebuke (hard), exhort (warm). Only the first two is a bludgeon; only the third is a comfortable fraud.

Patience and teaching. Patience, because people change slowly. Teaching, because reproof without instruction leaves a man knowing he is wrong but not what is right.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor’s Saturday: the week’s preparation is a sworn charge.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching but gather teachers to suit their passions.

Losing the appetite. Not that the truth is refuted, but that it becomes unbearable.

Itching ears. The itch is in the hearers. Paul puts demand before supply: we usually blame bad teachers for bad churches, but the market comes first.

For themselves. They are not passively misled; they go out and assemble a collection.

Turn and wander. One motion. No one who stops listening to the truth stays neutral.

On a Tuesday. You can now gather teachers who agree with you more easily than ever, and call it discernment. Test: when did one of your teachers last tell you something you did not want to hear?

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must stay sober, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist and fulfil his ministry.

Sober-minded. Clear-headed while others chase novelty.

Endure suffering. Said so often by now that Timothy cannot claim he was not warned.

An evangelist’s work. Timothy’s post was mostly corrective, and maintenance can swallow a ministry. Keep announcing the good news to people who have not heard. It is called work, a task to be done.

Is “evangelist” an office? Christ gives evangelists to the church (Ephesians 4:11), like Philip (Acts 21:8). Not all are so gifted, but every believer must be ready to speak of Christ (1 Peter 3:15).

Your ministry. Not Paul’s. Timothy need not be a second Paul. Finish what you were given (compare Colossians 4:17).

On a Tuesday. A dying apostle’s final orders are a short list any Christian could follow.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s life is already being poured out, and his departure is near.

A drink offering. Wine poured over a sacrifice already burning: the last, smallest act. In Philippians 2:17 it was “even if”. Now the condition is gone.

Departure. Analysis: untying a boat, striking a tent, unyoking an ox, freeing a prisoner. Every use implies somewhere to go.

Reclassified. Rome thinks it is disposing of a troublemaker. Paul describes a priest at an altar.

Composure. No panic, no resignation. Next he asks for his coat.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing death, or sitting with someone who is, this is the Christian vocabulary for it: offering and departure, not ending.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering of wine was poured out over a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith.

Perfect tense. Done, and the result stands.

The good fight. The contest of the arena, the charge he gave Timothy (1 Timothy 6:12). The fight was good: worth entering, whether or not every round was won.

Finished the race. What he wanted at Miletus years before (Acts 20:24), he now has.

Kept the faith. Both kept faith, like a promise, and guarded the faith, the deposit (1:14). The second is primary here.

Not a boast. The man who said grace was given before the ages, not for works (1:9), and called himself the foremost of sinners, is giving a steward’s report.

On a Tuesday. Few reach the end sure what their life was for. Ask now what God has given you to do, and do it.

verseByVerse.quote: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crown of righteousness awaits him and all who love Christ’s appearing.

Laid up. Reserved, already there with his name on it.

Crown of righteousness. The victor’s wreath, consisting of righteousness: final, full rightness with God, as gift.

The righteous judge. Unlike the one in Rome. Paul does not deny the injustice; he appeals it to a higher court and waits.

A crown for works? Some see here merit earning reward. But the Judge awards what grace has produced; the crown is given, and to all who love his appearing.

All who have loved his appearing. Not only apostles and martyrs. Anyone who has longed to see Christ.

For worship. A person shows what he loves by what he hopes is coming. Do you want him to come?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly. Demas, in love with this world, has deserted him; Crescens and Titus have gone elsewhere; only Luke is with him. Timothy is to bring Mark, who is useful, and the cloak, books and parchments Paul left at Troas. Alexander the metalworker did him great harm and Timothy should beware of him. At Paul’s first hearing no one stood by him, but the Lord stood with him and gave him strength so the message was fully proclaimed to the Gentiles, and he was rescued; the Lord will rescue him from every evil and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom. Paul sends greetings, asks Timothy to come before winter, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Wrong, Two Different Prayers

Of Alexander Paul says only that the Lord will repay (v.14); of the friends who deserted him he prays ‘may it not be charged against them’ (v.16) — Stephen's prayer (Acts 7:60), prayed thirty years on by the man who once held the coats.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demas left for love of this present world; Mark, once refused, is sent for as ‘very useful’ (vv.10–11).

Now: Five verses after the crown of righteousness, Paul asks for his cloak and his books (v.13): faith that does not pretend the body's needs are beneath notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges Timothy to come soon, for Demas has deserted him, and only Luke is with him.

Come soon. After the crown, this. He is lonely.

Demas. An insider (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24). Not heresy or scandal: he fell in love with this present age. That is how most people leave: not with a repudiation but with a preference.

Was he ever saved? Scripture does not tell us his end. If he never returned, he showed he had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19); Arminian Christians would see a believer who fell away. He may have repented. Either way, a warning.

Only Luke. Five words. The physician who survived the shipwreck with Paul is still there.

Mark. The deserter Paul refused to take (Acts 15:37–39), now sent for as “useful”. Barnabas was right, and Paul says so. Grace restores the failed, and those who gave up on them.

A textual note. Some important manuscripts read “Gaul” instead of “Galatia” for Crescens. Galatia is better attested; the words were close, and “Galatia” was sometimes used of Gaul.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you wrote off whom you should now ask for by name?
verseByVerse.note: Mark, who had once deserted Paul, is now “very useful.” Dalmatia lay on the Adriatic coast.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks for his cloak and his books, especially the parchments.

Eternity and being cold. Five verses after the crown.

The cloak. A heavy travelling cape, the one a poor man owned, probably left in a hurried arrest. A Roman prison in winter (v. 21) is serious for a man in his sixties.

The parchments. Costly vellum, most likely Scripture. A man who has finished the race sends across the empire for something to read, and Scripture most of all.

Tyndale. In his cell at Vilvoorde, about to be strangled and burned, he asked for a warmer cap, a woollen shirt, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary.

What it does not mean. Faith does not float above the body. Paul is not too heavenly-minded to ask for a coat.

On a Tuesday. Visiting someone in prison or a care home? Ask what they need. Sometimes it is a coat and a book.
verseByVerse.note: With winter coming (v. 21), Paul wants his heavy cloak; the parchments may have been copies of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alexander did Paul great harm; Timothy must beware of him.

Great harm. Unspecified; perhaps he informed on Paul.

Will repay. The better manuscripts have a plain future, not the wish “may the Lord reward him” (KJV). Paul is not cursing but stating what God will do.

Handing over the account. He neither pretends it was nothing nor retaliates. “Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Romans 12:19). A Christian can let an injury go because someone better placed will deal with it.

Two prayers. For the friends who failed him, “may it not be charged”; for Alexander, God will repay. Cowardice and malice are treated differently.

Beware. Forgiveness does not require naivety. Warning a colleague about a dangerous person is protection, not gossip.

On a Tuesday. When you have been badly wronged, write the name down, give it to God in prayer, and leave it with him.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At his first defence all deserted Paul, but the Lord stood by him and will bring him safely to his kingdom.

No one. At a preliminary hearing, a defendant’s friends would speak for him. None came.

Stephen’s prayer. “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). Paul watched it prayed while he held the coats; thirty years later, deserted, he prays it himself. He does not excuse them; he asks that it not be charged.

But the Lord stood by me. The support he was owed and did not get was supplied by someone else, in the same room.

So that the message. Strengthened not for acquittal but to preach, at his own capital trial.

The lion’s mouth. A proverbial danger (Psalm 22:21). He survived the hearing.

Rescue through death. He knows he will die. The rescue he expects is through the execution into the kingdom. Christian confidence does not say nothing bad will happen, but that nothing can stop the arrival.

For worship. When everyone leaves, the Lord stands by.
verseByVerse.note: The “first defense” was a preliminary hearing at his trial.

parallels.desc: Save me from the mouth of the lion

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends final greetings and asks Timothy to come before winter.

Prisca and Aquila. Old friends who once risked their necks for him (Romans 16:3–4). The wife is named first, as often.

Onesiphorus’s household. Perhaps he had died.

Trophimus left ill. Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11), could not heal a friend at will. Continuationists would say healing still depends on God’s will; cessationists see the sign-gifts already fading. Either way, healing was never a technique the apostles could operate.

Before winter. Shipping closed from about November to March. Paul is counting weeks. We do not know if Timothy made it.

Those who stayed. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia: Roman Christians who kept company with a condemned man when Demas would not. Irenaeus later names a Linus as the first leader of the Roman church after the apostles.

A textual note. Many manuscripts expand to “the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” and add “Amen”. The shorter text is earlier.

The last word. Singular to Timothy, then plural to all. Paul’s last written word is grace.
verseByVerse.note: Winter closed the Mediterranean to shipping, so Timothy had to sail before it. Paul had healed others, yet left Trophimus ill.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom:<sup>2</sup>preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.<sup>3</sup>For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions,<sup>4</sup>and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.<sup>5</sup>As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.<sup>6</sup>For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.<sup>7</sup>I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.<sup>8</sup>Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.<sup>9</sup>Do your best to come to me soon.<sup>10</sup>For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.<sup>11</sup>Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry.<sup>12</sup>Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.<sup>13</sup>When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.<sup>14</sup>Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds.<sup>15</sup>Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.<sup>16</sup>At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them!<sup>17</sup>But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion's mouth.<sup>18</sup>The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>19</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.<sup>20</sup>Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus.<sup>21</sup>Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers.<sup>22</sup>The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
